name: Satisficing (Bounded Rationality)
description: Rather than finding the best option, people often search until they find one that meets an aspiration level and stop. This is Herbert Simon's account of decision-making under limited time, information and computing ability.
design_relevance_note: Why users take the first good-enough option and skim rather than compare; design for scannable, defensible defaults rather than assuming users will optimise.
myth_risk_note: Easily misread as 'people are irrational'; the evidence says satisficing is often an effective response to uncertainty.
prevalence_note: Central to behavioural economics and UX writing on scanning and defaults.

findings.description: A survey of more than 60 years of research on satisficing (searching for an option that meets an aspiration level rather than optimising) identifies two traditions: under risk, satisficing is typically inferior to optimisation; under uncertainty, empirically derived satisficing strategies can be highly effective. The authors show conditions under which satisficing can be rational.

Eye-movement analysis of web-text skim-reading under time pressure found readers explicitly direct attention to the most important information and improve memory-test performance as a result, achieved by 'satisficing' -- reading a section until the rate of information gain drops below a threshold, then skipping ahead to the next section. Gaze patterns at both paragraph and page level supported this explanation, offering an independent mechanistic account for declining-attention reading patterns on web pages.
findings.source_venue: Proceedings of the SIGCHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '11)
